$comment: Rules protecting the framework itself. Standard 29. Their subject is this repository and any project that adopts it — not an analysis document.
$note: integrity.no-weakening is the fifth and last non-exemptible rule. The other four are the fabrication-and-guarantee prohibitions in rules/prohibited.json. test/integrity.test.mjs asserts that set is exactly those five, so removing a flag fails a test rather than quietly widening what may be waived.

rules.title: No standard, test, or verification mechanism is weakened to permit a desired conclusion
rules.description: No standard, test, applicability determination, evidence requirement, or verification mechanism is bypassed, weakened, removed, reclassified, reinterpreted, falsified, or manipulated solely because it prevents a desired implementation or conclusion.
rules.rationale: The cheapest way to pass any check is to change the check. Without this rule every other rule in the catalog is advisory, because the same commit that violates one can remove it.
rules.remediation: Restore what was changed. If the standard is genuinely wrong, change it for that reason and record the reason — a change that would still be correct if the blocked outcome were not wanted is legitimate, and the record is what lets a reviewer tell the difference.
rules.$assuranceNote: NONE, and the reasoning is worth stating because a case for 'partial' is available and wrong. The mechanical forms of weakening — reworded quotations, deleted guards, respelled rule ids, waived non-exemptible rules, stale attestations — ARE caught, but they are caught by integrity.guards-present, which is a separate structural rule that claims full assurance for exactly that. Crediting this rule for the same coverage would count it twice and overstate what THIS check establishes. This rule's evaluator is a human, and an automated run establishes nothing about it. The motivated forms are not caught at all: judging whether a change was made SOLELY because a standard was in the way requires reading intent, and no checker does. A standard rewritten wholesale, with its quotations intact and its requirements gutted, passes every automated check in this repository.

rules.title: Every mechanical guard is wired into CI
rules.description: Each guard named in Standard 29's protection table exists as a script and runs as a CI step, before the step that renders a verdict.
rules.rationale: A guard that is not run is not a guard. Commenting out a CI step is the least visible way to disable a check, because the script it calls remains in the repository looking intact.
rules.remediation: Restore the missing step or script. If a guard is genuinely obsolete, remove it and its entry in Standard 29 in the same change, with the reason recorded.
rules.$assuranceNote: FULL, and legitimately so: this is a structural check with an exact answer. The workflow either contains the step and the script exists, or it does not. What it does NOT establish is that the guard works — only that it runs. Whether each guard actually catches its defect is established by the mutation tests, which are a separate exercise.

rules.title: A rule is never removed or respelled without a resolvable trace
rules.description: A rule id that has been published remains resolvable — through the rule itself or through an alias — and any deprecation carries its lifecycle fields.
rules.rationale: A rule that vanishes takes every policy declaration about it with it, and the project's exceptions and applicability claims silently stop referring to anything. Renaming has the same effect while looking like tidying.
rules.remediation: Keep the old id resolvable as an alias, and record deprecatedIn, supersededBy, and removedIn rather than deleting the entry.
rules.$assuranceNote: PARTIAL. The catalog loader enforces that lifecycle fields are present and that aliases do not collide, which is checked exactly. It cannot detect a rule deleted outright in the same change that removes every reference to it — that leaves nothing behind to notice.
